prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Just now I touched my chest And felt my heart quivering there. This must be one of the bad times. I think it is quivering with remorse And exhaustion. Once I saw a heart Beating in a documentary. I was a very Little girl and the sight disgusted me. Throbbing and not stopping my heart betrays Me and yet remains sure and true, a thing Of nature. Earth bleeding Its guts out on the sea floor exhausts Me with remorse and shame, and yet I have to trust it As wealth is proven by how terribly it devastates Itself, and I am but one symptom among billions of the wealth Of Earth. A tired feeling that is recuperated by a passing spaceship Or an infinitude like fame but more universal. I will have to miss you Earth; I miss you already. And yet when I touch myself whom I should Not trust it is still only the heaviest and most jealous feelings that bind me to you, like blood.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Just, And, This

outputs.L1:
Just now, I touched my chest  
and felt my heart quivering there.  
This must be one of the bad times.  
I think it is quivering with remorse  
and exhaustion.

Once, I saw a heart  
beating in a documentary.  
I was a very little girl,  
and the sight disgusted me.  
Throbbing without ceasing, my heart betrays  
me, and yet remains steadfast and true—  
a thing of nature.

Earth, bleeding  
its guts onto the seafloor, exhausts  
me with remorse and shame, and yet I have to trust it,  
as wealth is proven by how terribly it devastates  
itself, and I am but one symptom among billions of the wealth  
of Earth.

A tired feeling, recuperated by a passing spaceship,  
or by an infinitude like fame, but more universal.  
I will have to miss you, Earth;  
I miss you already.

And yet, when I touch myself—whom I should  
not trust—it is still only the heaviest and most jealous feelings  
that bind me to you,  
like blood.
outputs.L2:
A moment ago, I placed my hand over my chest  
and sensed my heart trembling inside.  
This must be one of the difficult hours.  
I imagine it shakes from guilt  
and from being worn out.  

When I was a very small child,  
I once watched a heart  
pulsing in a documentary,  
and the image repelled me.  

My own heart keeps pounding,  
refusing to stop;  
it deceives me,  
and still it stays steady and faithful,  
something made by nature.  

The Earth, spilling its insides  
across the ocean floor,  
fills me with fatigue, remorse, and shame.  
Even so, I must believe in it,  
because its riches are shown  
by the awful force with which it destroys itself,  
and I am only one sign, among billions,  
of Earth’s abundance.  

It is a weariness restored  
by some passing spacecraft,  
or by an endlessness like fame,  
only larger and less human.  

Earth, I will have to long for you;  
I long for you already.  
And still, when I touch this self  
I know I ought not rely on,  
it is only the weightiest, most possessive feelings  
that fasten me to you—  
like blood.
outputs.L3:
The speaker feels their heart quivering and understands the sensation not simply as a physical irregularity, but as an emotional sign: a tremor of remorse, weariness, and strain. The body seems to reveal what the mind may not be able to fully admit. This trembling heart becomes a symbol of inner exhaustion, as though the speaker’s guilt and fatigue have settled into the flesh itself.

This unease recalls a childhood memory. The speaker remembers watching a documentary in which a human heart was shown beating, exposed in all its wet, muscular persistence. Rather than inspiring wonder, the sight produced disgust. The body appeared mechanical, relentless, and almost obscene in its natural obedience: pumping, contracting, continuing without permission or reflection. From an early age, the speaker was disturbed by the fact that life depends on such involuntary processes, on a hidden physical labor that never stops.

That private disgust with the body expands into a larger sorrow for the Earth. The speaker connects their own bodily unease to the planet’s devastation, as if the trembling of the heart echoes the damaged rhythms of the natural world. Their remorse is not only personal but planetary. They feel shame at belonging to a species, and perhaps to a form of life, that participates in the Earth’s suffering. The planet’s wounds seem to become internal wounds; its exhaustion is mirrored in the speaker’s own.

At the same time, Earth is portrayed as a place of overwhelming wealth and abundance. Yet this richness cannot be separated from violence and destruction. The planet’s fertility, beauty, and power are bound up with its ability to erupt, decay, consume, and devastate itself. Creation and ruin are not opposites here; they are part of the same vast process. The speaker sees themselves as only a tiny symptom of that abundance—one small, troubled expression of the Earth’s excess, vitality, and self-destructive force.

Even so, the speaker cannot detach from the world they mourn. They mistrust the self, feel sorrow for the planet, and recognize the heaviness of their own emotions, but they remain deeply bound to Earth. Their attachment is not light or peaceful. It is heavy, jealous, intimate, and bodily—like blood. The connection is painful, but it is also inescapable. The speaker belongs to the Earth not through innocence or comfort, but through guilt, desire, grief, and the shared pulse of living matter.
outputs.L4:
The poem begins in the body, with the speaker’s attention fixed on the quivering heart. This physical image immediately suggests fear, vulnerability, and a loss of control. The heart is not presented as a stable center of feeling, but as something unsettled and exposed. From this intimate bodily anxiety, the poem widens outward toward the Earth itself, imagining the planet as damaged, unstable, and even self-devastating. In this movement from the speaker’s inner life to ecological destruction, the poem connects personal distress with planetary crisis. The speaker’s remorse and disgust are not only private emotions; they become part of a larger atmosphere of environmental grief.

As the poem expands further, it introduces images of cosmic distance, making the Earth appear small, isolated, and fragile. This shift in scale intensifies the speaker’s sense of helplessness. Seen from a cosmic perspective, human suffering may seem insignificant, yet the poem does not allow the speaker to escape the weight of feeling. Instead, the vastness of space makes the speaker’s attachment to Earth feel even more painful and urgent. The planet is damaged and compromised, but it is also the only home the speaker knows.

Throughout the poem, the speaker struggles with shame, mistrust, and revulsion toward the self. The body becomes a site of anxiety, as if human feeling itself were contaminated by the same destructive forces that have harmed the Earth. Yet the poem does not reject feeling altogether. Even disgust and remorse reveal a continuing bond with the world. The speaker’s pain proves that they are still connected to the planet they mourn. In this way, the poem presents human emotion as both a symptom of ecological damage and a form of belonging. To feel grief for the Earth is to be implicated in its devastation, but it is also to remain intimately tied to it.
outputs.L5:
Just as every story begins with a single thought, this one begins with three simple words: **Just, And, This**.

**Just** reminds us to focus on what is fair, honest, and necessary. It can mean doing the right thing, even when it is difficult. It can also mean simplicity—just one step, just one choice, just one moment at a time.

**And** is a word of connection. It joins ideas, people, and possibilities. It reminds us that life is rarely made of one thing alone. There is hope and challenge, effort and reward, learning and growth.

**This** brings our attention to the present. Not yesterday, not tomorrow, but this moment. This chance. This decision. This opportunity to begin again or continue moving forward.

Together, these words can form a quiet message: **Just and this**—be fair, stay connected, and pay attention to the present. Sometimes, the simplest words can carry the deepest meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in a confessional, contemporary style about touching your chest, feeling your heart, and connecting bodily shame to ecological grief and love for Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
I put my hand on my chest  
like I’m trying to calm an animal  
I have kept indoors too long.

There it is—  
the small engine,  
the wet fist,  
the stubborn drum  
refusing every story I’ve told it  
about being unworthy.

I used to hate this body  
for being so visible,  
so needy,  
for asking for softness  
in a world that rewards the blade.

I learned shame early:  
how to fold myself smaller,  
how to apologize for hunger,  
how to make a mirror  
into a weather report  
and call every forecast my fault.

But tonight my palm warms  
against my ribs  
and I think of the Earth—  
how we have touched her  
without tenderness,  
taken from her chest  
and called it progress.

Forests felled like hair  
we were embarrassed to grow.  
Rivers thick with the things  
we could not admit we wanted.  
The sky holding its fever  
above us, blue and bruised,  
still making room for birds.

Maybe my shame  
is not separate  
from the grief I feel  
when another species disappears  
quietly as a secret.

Maybe I was taught  
to treat my body  
the way we treat the planet:  
as a problem to solve,  
a resource to mine,  
a wilderness to manage  
into obedience.

But my heart keeps knocking.  
Not politely.  
Not with permission.  
It says:  
you are made of the same water  
that remembers glaciers,  
the same salt as ancient seas.  
Your breath is borrowed  
from leaves.  
Your bones are a brief arrangement  
of minerals dreaming they are a person.

So I press harder,  
not to punish,  
but to listen.

Under my hand,  
the body I have blamed  
goes on living.  
Under our cities,  
the mycelium threads its dark gospel.  
In the burned field,  
green insists.  
In the oily harbor,  
a gull lifts  
its impossible white body  
into morning.

I don’t know how to save anything  
without first loving  
what I was told  
to be ashamed of.

So I start here:  
palm to sternum,  
breath to breath,  
a private weather changing.

I say to my heart,  
I’m sorry.

I say to the Earth,  
I’m sorry.

And because apology  
is only the first seed,  
I stay.  
I keep my hand there.  
I feel the pulse  
answering the pulse  
beneath soil, beneath pavement,  
beneath all our bright damage—

love,  
not clean,  
not innocent,  
but alive,

still alive,

asking what we will do  
with our tenderness now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal lyric poem where the speaker feels their heart quivering, remembers seeing a beating heart as a child, and then reflects on the Earth bleeding at the ocean floor.
counterfactuals.output:
My heart quivers tonight—  
a moth trapped in the red lamp of my ribs,  
brushing its powder against the bone.

I remember being small,  
lifted toward a table of silver weather,  
where a heart lay beating by itself—  
not dead, not living,  
a wet fist opening and closing  
as if trying to remember  
the hand it belonged to.

It spoke without a mouth.  
It knocked on the air.  
I heard my own name  
inside its crimson trembling.

Since then, every pulse  
has been a doorway ajar,  
every silence a room  
where something tender is working  
in the dark.

And now I think of the Earth,  
vast animal under our feet,  
rolling in its sleep  
while deep below the oceans  
its wounds glow open—

black smokers, mineral blood,  
iron and sulfur pouring  
from the torn seams of the world.

There, where no sun arrives,  
the planet bleeds upward  
into cold water,  
and strange white creatures gather  
like prayers around the injury.

O trembling heart,  
O childhood lantern,  
O blue globe with its hidden arteries—

what is a life  
but a wound learning rhythm,  
a darkness  
beating itself into light?
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a melancholic prose-poem about remorse, exhaustion, the human body as part of planetary destruction, and the feeling of already missing Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
I am tired in the old mineral way, as if the bones have been quarried from mountains and the mountains are still grieving their loss. My hands smell faintly of gasoline, oranges, rain that could not cleanse anything. I have carried so much convenience through the day that by evening my body feels crowded with small crimes: plastic in the blood, smoke in the lungs, hunger arranged in bright packaging, a blue light burning where the stars should be.

Forgive me, Earth, though forgiveness is another thing I have wanted from you without earning it. I have slept under roofs made from forests and warmed myself with buried summers. I have eaten from fields that forgot their insects, drunk from rivers traveling under names of poison, loved my little life with an animal desperation while the coral paled and the glaciers loosened their ancient grip.

There is no innocence in the body. It breathes what has been burned. It asks for heat, for transport, for fruit out of season, for the soft violence of comfort. Even my sorrow consumes: the lamp above the desk, the server holding these words, the kettle grieving steam into the room. I am made of appetite and ash. I am not separate from the ruin; I am one of its walking organs.

And still—how I will miss it. How I already miss it, even with my feet upon it. The wet leaf stuck to the pavement. The moth trembling at the window. The smell of soil after rain, rising like a memory from a future where no one is left to breathe it in. I miss the planet as if it were a childhood house we are burning while still inside, each room filling with smoke, each photograph curling at the edges.

The sky tonight is bruised purple over the city, tender and exhausted. Planes cross it like stitches that never close. Somewhere, a whale turns in the dark with a song older than our machines. Somewhere, trees labor quietly at the edge of a highway, taking into themselves what we cannot bear to name.

I want to lie down on the ground and apologize with the whole weight of me. I want to become small enough to be forgiven by moss. But the body keeps going—mouth, furnace, engine, need. The heart beats its red fist against the ribs, not noble, not guilty enough to stop, only alive.

And this is the worst of it: to love what we have wounded. To stand on the beloved and feel it warming beneath us, fevered, finite. To understand too late that Earth was never a backdrop, never an inheritance, never an endless mother with endless milk, but a body like ours—breathable, breakable, already missing what it used to be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original poem in the style of a modern experimental poet, blending visceral anatomy, environmental devastation, wealth, spaceships, fame, and a jealous attachment to the planet.
counterfactuals.output:
**EARTH, MY GLITTERING WOUND**

I keep my planet in my mouth  
like a stolen tooth.

All night the billionaires rehearse departure—  
silver darts in the ulcered sky,  
ships sleek as surgical instruments,  
ships with champagne engines,  
ships named after mothers  
they have not called.

Below, the forests cough up black lace.  
Rivers drag their green intestines  
through the open pit of morning.  
The reef, that cathedral of calcium,  
bleaches itself into applause.

Everyone famous is leaving beautifully.

Their faces bloom on every screen:  
skin like refrigerated fruit,  
teeth like small clean colonies.  
They wave from the launchpad  
in tailored fireproof innocence  
while the crowd hums like a wound  
pretending to be a choir.

And I—  
I am jealous.

Not of the rockets, no,  
not of the velvet gravity of money,  
not of the orbital suites  
where the rich will sip blue light  
from glasses thinner than guilt.

I am jealous for the mud.

For the worm’s wet braid.  
For the lung-pink dawn  
opening over a refinery.  
For the mangrove’s knuckled hand  
still gripping the drowned edge.  
For every ugly, beloved acre  
we have bitten and called progress.

Earth, don’t look at them.

Look at me.

I will press my ear  
to your fevered crust  
and hear the magma muttering  
like blood behind a bruise.

I will wear your weather  
until my ribs rust.

Let the famous ascend  
in their immaculate coffins,  
let their names orbit  
like perfume around a corpse.

I want the dirt under my nails  
to know me by pressure.  
I want the storm to enter  
without knocking.  
I want to be ruined here,  
locally, terrestrially,  
with the animals and ash,

clutching the planet  
as if love were a body  
and the body  
were burning

and still mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw, intimate poem beginning with “Just now I touched my chest” that turns into a meditation on trust, shame, ecological collapse, and the blood-like bond between self and Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
Just now I touched my chest  
as if checking whether I was still inside it,  
as if the heart were a small animal  
I had betrayed and needed to coax back  
with two fingers, a whisper,  
the old promise: I’m here.

But trust has never come easily to me.  
Not in hands. Not in rooms.  
Not in the mirror with its blunt weather.  
There is a shame I carry  
like damp clothing under my skin—  
the shame of needing,  
the shame of surviving,  
the shame of having turned away  
from my own tenderness  
so many times  
it stopped lifting its face.

Outside, the world is burning  
with the same quiet I have used  
to burn myself.  
Forests become breathless.  
Rivers thicken with our forgetting.  
The sea rises like grief  
that has finally stopped asking permission.  
Everywhere, the Earth is showing us  
her bruises, her fevers,  
her animals vanishing into our appetite,  
her soil split open  
like a mouth saying  
enough.

And still, my blood moves.  
Red, ancient, tidal.  
Iron singing its dark hymn  
from the center of me  
to the center of everything.  
How could I believe I am separate  
from the wounded ground  
when my body is only borrowed weather,  
salt, carbon, water, ash?  
When my pulse keeps time  
with roots pushing through ruined dirt,  
with whales carrying cathedrals of song  
through poisoned blue,  
with the last bees entering blossoms  
as if love were still a fact?

I touch my chest again.  
Not to accuse it.  
Not to ask why it failed  
to be clean, fearless, untouched.  
I touch it the way rain touches dust—  
with no interest in shame.  
I touch it because trust may begin  
as nothing more than this:  
a palm laid gently  
over the red door of the body,  
a listening.

Earth, I have treated you  
the way I treated myself—  
as if you would always forgive  
without needing repair.  
As if your silence meant consent.  
As if abundance were not a body  
with limits.  
I am sorry  
for all the ways I learned to live  
by taking.

But sorrow is not enough.  
A wound does not close  
because we name it.  
So let my blood remember yours.  
Let the river in me  
answer the river outside me.  
Let my breath become accountable  
to leaf, lung, cloud, and creature.  
Let me be ashamed only long enough  
to turn toward the damage  
with my hands open.

Just now I touched my chest  
and felt, beneath the bone,  
not innocence,  
not absolution,  
but a small red trust  
still moving—  
the Earth inside me  
refusing to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
